John Paul II. Born Karol Wojtyła, he reigned as pope from 1978 to 2005 and was the first non-Italian pope in 455 years. He was also the second-longest reigning pope in history. One of the most traveled world leaders in history, he used his global influence to support human rights and speak out against political oppression.

He helped dismantle Soviet-bloc communism in Eastern Europe, particularly in his native Poland. His 1979 visit to Poland and public support energized the anti-communist Solidarity movement, which played a key role in the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe. In 1981, he survived an assassination attempt in St. Peter's Square when Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Ağca shot him. He later visited his would-be assassin in prison and forgave him.

During his pontificate, John Paul traveled extensively, visiting 129 countries and establishing World Youth Day in 1985 to foster youth ministry. In 1992, he issued the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the first comprehensive codification of Catholic belief in over four centuries. He also delivered a series of lectures known as the Theology of the Body. During the Jubilee Year 2000, he apologized for the historical errors of the Catholic Church, including the trial of Galileo, the Crusades, the Inquisition, and Christian involvement in the Holocaust.
